1.definition: The steppe nomads China had expelled in 1368 but who remained a standing threat on the northern land frontier — one of the reasons the Ming court turned its attention and money away from the sea.

The large central-and-western Spanish kingdom, Portugal's powerful neighbor and perennial rival, forever threatening to swallow the smaller country — the threat that helped forge the restless Aviz dynasty.
The Muslim Berber dynasty ruling Morocco when Portugal stormed Ceuta in 1415; the port had been the Mediterranean terminus of its trans-Saharan gold trade.

2.definition: Sailing a zigzag course to make progress against the wind — angling close to the oncoming wind on one side, then turning and angling back the other way. The lateen sail made it possible and was the key to coming home down the African coast.

The steady winds that blow from the northeast toward the equator in the North Atlantic, pushing a ship southwest toward Africa — half of the great clockwise wind loop the Portuguese learned to ride with the volta do mar.

The prevailing winds that blow from the west across the higher latitudes of the North Atlantic, carrying a homebound ship northeast back to Europe — the return half of the wind loop the Azores sat squarely within.

3.definition: The West African gold empire that dominated the trans-Saharan trade in the 1300s, so rich its emperor Mansa Musa reportedly crashed the price of gold in Cairo by giving so much away on pilgrimage.

The fabled trading and scholarly city on the bend of the Niger River, famed for its libraries and Islamic learning — a symbol of the wealth and sophistication of the West African interior the Portuguese were trying to reach by sea.

A port in the Algarve, southern Portugal (not the Nigerian city), where a fleet returned in 1444 with some 235 enslaved Africans who were auctioned on the dock — the event usually marked as the start of the European Atlantic slave trade.

4.definition: An ancient Christian kingdom in the Horn of Africa, the real realm later identified with the legend of Prester John. The Portuguese spy Covilhã eventually reached it and lived out his life at its court.
The pepper-growing southwestern coast of India, the destination Covilhã scouted by land and the goal toward which all the Portuguese sea voyages were aimed.

The name Bartolomeu Dias gave the great rocky promontory at the bottom of Africa for the gale that blew him around it in 1488; King John II renamed it the Cape of Good Hope once he grasped it had opened the sea road to the East.

5.definition: The Italian maritime port-republic where Columbus was born and learned his trade; one of the merchant cities that grew rich reselling Eastern spices and that the new sea routes would eventually ruin.

King of Aragon whose 1469 marriage to Isabella of Castile fused the two great crowns of Spain into a single power; together they were the Catholic Monarchs who finished the Reconquista and gambled on Columbus.
The chain of low Caribbean islands where Columbus made his first landfall in October 1492, on an island the Taíno called Guanahani and he renamed San Salvador, believing it lay off the coast of Asia.

6.matchText: supreme head of the Catholic Church
6.definition: The head of the Catholic Church, who under the prevailing theory of the day could grant Christian monarchs the right to seize non-Christian lands in exchange for converting their inhabitants — the legal fiction underpinning the whole carve-up.

The eastern bulge of South America that Cabral's fleet bumped into in 1500 while swinging wide on the volta do mar — and which, by luck, fell on the Portuguese side of the Tordesillas line, the reason Brazil speaks Portuguese today.

7.definition: Almeida's ruthless successor and the true architect of Portugal's Asian empire, who reasoned that tiny Portugal should seize and fortify the ocean's choke-points rather than try to conquer territory — taking Goa, Malacca, and Hormuz in a swift, violent sequence.

One of the wealthy stone-built Muslim merchant cities of the East African Swahili coast — alongside Malindi, Kilwa, and Mozambique — plugged into the Indian Ocean trade for centuries before the Portuguese arrived as ragged interlopers.

A trading hub where goods are warehoused and re-exported rather than consumed locally — the role of Malacca, which commanded the strait through which all the spice trade of the islands beyond had to flow.

8.definition: The narrow neck of land joining North and South America, which Balboa hacked across in 1513 to become the first European to see the Pacific from the American side.

The largest single feature on Earth, covering roughly a third of the planet, which Magellan named for its deceptive calm after the chaos of his strait — and which then nearly killed his crew over a three-month crossing with no land.
A revolt of a ship's crew or officers against their commander. Magellan crushed one by his resentful Spanish captains with executions and maroonings as the fleet wintered in the bleak far south.
The Southeast Asian island group where Magellan's starving fleet finally found food in 1521 — and where he was killed at Mactan, two-thirds of the way around the world.

The chieftain of Mactan who refused to submit to Spanish overlordship and whose warriors cut Magellan down in the surf in 1521. Today he is a national hero in the Philippines — the first indigenous leader remembered for defeating the Europeans.

9.definition: The band of central and southern Mexico and northern Central America where a long line of civilizations — Olmec, Maya, Mexica and others — shared gods, calendars, ballgames, and pyramid-temples over thousands of years.

10.definition: The long mountain spine running down the western edge of South America, along whose 2,500-mile length the Inca built the largest empire the Americas ever produced.

The bloody succession war between Huayna Capac's sons Atahualpa and Huáscar, touched off when smallpox killed the emperor and his heir — leaving the empire exhausted and divided at the exact moment Pizarro arrived.
The coastal capital the Spanish founded in Peru, besieged by an Inca army during Manco Inca's great 1536 rebellion.

11.definition: The large, standardized Spanish silver coin worth eight reales (the peso de ocho or Spanish dollar) — abundant and reliably pure, it became the closest thing the early-modern world had to a universal currency, circulating from Canton to Boston.

12.definition: The Catholic Church's machinery for detecting and punishing heresy through interrogation, denunciation, torture, and execution. Spain and Portugal carried it overseas; the Goa Inquisition policed converts suspected of secretly keeping their old faith.

A member of the Catholic preaching order founded by St. Dominic. Dominican friars like Montesinos and Las Casas, living among the dying indigenous peoples, became the loudest voices of conscience against the conquest.

13.definition: The broad river leading deep into the North American interior that Cartier sailed from 1534 and Champlain anchored New France upon; from a local word kanata (village) the name Canada eventually came.

14.definition: The nightmare ocean crossing of the triangular trade, in which African captives were packed into slave ships and carried to be sold in the Americas; well over a million died in the passage itself.

The Flemish cartographer who in 1569 devised a way of projecting the round Earth onto a flat map so a constant compass bearing came out as a straight line — a navigator's dream, still behind most maps you've seen.
The Flemish mapmaker who in 1570 bound uniform maps of the whole known Earth into the Theatrum Orbis Terrarum, the first true atlas — a planet a person could hold in one book.
